Minakshi, put the kettle on and sit. You're about to choose a health policy, so let me tell you how I did it. I'm Trisha.
The agent who phoned me was smooth. "Just sign today, it's the best." I said no and took the brochures home.
I made a table. Down one side, several insurers; across, the things that matter: how much cover, how long before certain things are covered, the limit on room rent, what is left out, and how often the company actually settles claims. Then I read the small print, line by line, with a pencil.
Two policies that looked alike turned out very different on room rent and exclusions. That saved me from a nasty surprise.
The agent called back twice. I just said I'd decided.

Maria's company health cover would end in ten days when she switched jobs, and the new employer's cover wouldn't start for three months. The sales calls began at once. One agent rang four times, promising "best plan, everything covered, sign today".
Instead of signing, Maria made a checklist with her friend Sarika, who had once had a claim rejected: cover amount, waiting periods for existing conditions, room rent limit, exclusions, and each insurer's record of settling claims.
With the clock ticking, they split the work. Sarika pulled the claim-settlement figures from the regulator's published reports. Maria downloaded four policy documents and read the exclusions section of each, even though it made her eyes ache.
The "everything covered" plan had a room-rent limit so low that a normal hospital room would mean paying the difference herself. Another had a four-year waiting period. On day eight, Maria chose the third plan, with a higher premium but fewer traps, and paid online before the deadline.

qa.q: How many policy documents did Maria download?
What was Maria feeling as the sales calls kept coming?
qa.a: Maria felt pressured but wary, choosing to check the details instead of signing that day.
It compared the same key points across insurers, so hidden limits like the low room-rent cap showed up clearly.

Sudha's parents in Pune had never had health insurance, and after her father's short hospital stay last year, she decided to buy a family policy herself. Her colleague Aditi forwarded an ad: "Cheapest cover in India!"
Sudha didn't click it. That evening at her desk in the Hinjewadi office, she made a table with five columns: cover amount, waiting period for existing illnesses, room rent limit, exclusions, and how reliably each insurer pays claims. Then she filled it in for five insurers, reading each policy's fine print instead of the brochure.
The cheapest one excluded anything related to her father's blood pressure for four years. Another capped room rent so low that most private rooms would cost extra. By Friday, two policies were left. She sent the table to Aditi.
"I'd never have noticed the waiting period," Aditi wrote back. "Can I use your table?"

Why did Sudha decide to buy a policy herself?
qa.a: After her father's hospital stay, Sudha felt worried about her parents having no cover and wanted to protect them.

qa.q: Why is reading the fine print wiser than choosing the cheapest ad?
qa.a: The fine print showed traps like a four-year exclusion and a low room-rent cap that the ad would never mention.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Sudha's table?
qa.a: Aditi is impressed, admitting the waiting period would have gone unnoticed, and asks to use the table too.
